pr_body:
The `JsonNode.DeepEquals` implementation currently uses UTF-8 sequence equality when determining if two JSON numbers are equal. This means that under the current semantics `1.0` != `1` and `-0.0` != `0`. 

Following feedback from @gregsdennis I put up this PR that attempts to derive numeric equality from `decimal`. This approach has its own share of problems though because we currently have no way of handling numeric values not representable by `decimal`, so it still needs to fallback to sequence equality (a `BigDecimal` type might have been useful  in this case).

Fix #97490.

issue_context.title: `JsonNode.DeepEquals()` erroneously considers number representation
issue_context.body:
### Description

When a `JsonValue` with an integer value is compared to a `JsonValue` with a decimal that has been initialized with a zero fractional part, `object.Equals()` returns true, but `JsonValue.DeepEquals()` returns false.

In JSON, all numbers are treated equally, with arbitrary precision.  As such, `4` and `4.0` are equivalent JSON values.

### Reproduction Steps

```c#
public void Repro()
{
    JsonNode intFour = 4;
    JsonNode floatFour = 4.0m;

    Console.WriteLine("4 == 4.0:   {0}", 4 == 4.0m);  // true
    Console.WriteLine("DeepEquals: {0}", JsonNode.DeepEquals(intFour, floatFour));  // false
}
```

### Expected behavior

I expect both to return true.

### Actual behavior

`JsonValue.DeepEquals()` returns false.

### Regression?

No.  `JsonNode.DeepEquals()` is new to .Net 8.

### Known Workarounds

I have defined my own equality methods, published in _Json.More.Net_, but was hoping to be able to remove this functionality for .Net 8.

### Configuration

.Net 8 (any build), x64.

### Other information

_No response_

`4 == 4.0m` or `4.0m.Equals(4)` is converting the `int` to `decimal` with implicit conversion. The `object.Equals(object)` overload returns false.

If we take the concept that JSON has only one number type, how should we deal with the precision of `long`?

> `4 == 4.0m` or `4.0m.Equals(4)` is converting the `int` to `decimal` with implicit conversion. The `object.Equals(object)` overload returns false.

👍 Thanks.  I missed that.

> If we take the concept that JSON has only one number type, how should we deal with the precision of `long`?

You answered it: we take the concept that JSON has only one number type.

If the numerical value is the same, then they're JSON-equal.  I would expect this with any numeric type, including a bignum.

I would say that's a known limitation because of how `JsonNode` is implemented. It would be nice if we had a `JsonNumber`-like struct that exposes the correct equality semantics when it comes to handling js-like numeric values. Today we do this, which isn't great either from a correctness or performance standpoint:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/2558ff925b907633332c2f5160c15d153f29f2db/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Nodes/JsonValueOfT.cs#L119-L121

Yeah I initially did something similar, but considerably less efficient. I would `.ToString()` the two numbers and compare the output.

But recently, I figured out that `decimal` encodes the significant digits in order to output them again.  Thus with `decimal`s, 4 isn't exactly the same as 4.0 because their precision is different.

I've since moved on to this: https://github.com/gregsdennis/json-everything/blob/master/Json.More%2FJsonNodeExtensions.cs#L50-L52.  `.GetNumber()` extracts the value as a `decimal`, so now I'm doing a`decimal` equality check.  This limits me to the `decimal` value range, but I'm comfortable with that.
4 and 4.0 have different meanings in scientific notation. significant digits and the like. they could be converted to one another but should not be considered equal in scientific calculations.
Granted, and I don't disagree.  But I'm after JSON equality here.
They are equal in JavaScript which is what we should want to emulate.

review_comments: If the JSON erroneously included a +, is this going to assert? Or is this an assert because the parser before this point would have already failed and we'd never get here?
We expect the input to have already been validated by the JSON reader (this is being invoked by materialized `JsonElement` instances).

For three inputs like this, I'd just use this version everywhere rather than special-casing for SearchValues; I wouldn't expect SearchValues to be meaningfully better, especially given the expected size of the inputs being fed in here. (In fact, I'd need to double-check, but I believe today SearchValues on three bytes will just end up using this same API.)
Presumably this path is super rare?
Super rare is accurate. It requires significands exceeding 256 digits.
